title: AI Ad Agency Where You Own the Ads and the AI Actor Rights
summary: Owning ad files and owning an AI actor are separate rights. Compare Knowlify, EditClub, Pinprick, Valid and Arcads on usage terms, actor reuse and consent.
body_markdown:
## Pinprick and Valid: custom actors and cleared personas


[Pinprick](https://pinprick.io/ai-ugc-agency) casts AI actors per brand. Eligible brands, mainly those already spending meaningfully on ads, pay an agreed percentage of ad spend rather than a per-ad fee, and the rate is not published, as of October 2026. Media buying is scoped separately. Ask how the percentage is calculated and whether the cast stays with your brand after the contract ends.


[Valid](https://www.valid.co/ai-influencers) sells AI influencers, which it describes as AI-generated personas cleared for paid use with whitelisting included, as of October 2026. Its Performance Creative engagements require a two-month minimum and access to your ad accounts, and prices are not published. Cleared for paid use is a usage statement, not an ownership statement, so ask for the reuse terms in writing.


## Arcads: a library of AI actors and a software workflow


[Arcads](https://www.arcads.ai/) lists more than 1,000 AI actors, or lets you generate an actor that holds your product, shows your app or wears your clothes, as of October 2026. Arcads is also a software workflow to evaluate if you want to keep production in-house, so the rights check for each actor sits with your team.


The actor's source matters. Arcads'[FAQ](https://help.arcads.ai/en/articles/17350051-arcads-faq) says its talking actors are based on real actors who consented and are paid for their likeness, as of October 2026. That answers consent, not whether you can keep using the actor after your contract ends, so ask that separately.


## What does Meta require you to disclose?


Meta's[transparency update](https://about.fb.com/news/2025/02/gen-ai-transparency-metas-ads-products/) says it labels ads created or significantly edited with its own generative AI creative features. When those tools add a photorealistic AI-generated person, the label appears next to the Sponsored label, as of October 2026. Meta also says it will detect ads made with third-party AI tools and show an "AI info" label in About this ad, but the post does not say that detection is live yet.


Plan for the label whatever the rights terms say. A rights clause will not remove a disclosure that the platform applies.


## Two checks that rights clauses do not cover


A rights clause does not make a fake testimonial true. The[FTC's testimonial Q&A](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/consumer-reviews-testimonials-rule-questions-answers) says there is no blanket ban on AI-generated avatars in marketing, but an avatar is prohibited when the testimonial it delivers is fake or false, as of October 2026. Keep the presenter's lines to accurate product information, and never present a synthetic person as a real customer.


Copyright is a separate question. The[U.S. Copyright Office's AI resources](https://www.copyright.gov/ai/) treat digital replicas and the copyrightability of output as distinct issues. Ask for a rights record covering inputs and outputs, rather than accepting "AI-generated" as the whole answer. Our guide to[AI actors and likeness](https://knowlify.com/articles/ai-actors-and-likeness-celebrity-lookalikes-rights-copyright) covers consent and lookalike risk in more detail.


## A contract checklist for ads and actors


Turn the rights into clauses before the first brief:


- Final and source files: who owns them, in which formats, and for how long you can keep them.
- Actor: whether it is a library or custom actor, whether it is exclusive, and whether it can appear for other brands.
- Reuse after termination: whether existing ads can keep running, and what happens to the actor's look in future versions.
- Likeness and voice: the consent records behind any real person whose likeness or voice the actor is based on.
- Usage: paid, organic, whitelisting, duration and channels, and who handles AI disclosure.


Ask for a term sheet with these answers before a pilot. If a provider cannot state them in writing, treat the rights as unresolved, however good the first ad looks. Our[guide to vetting an AI ad agency](https://knowlify.com/articles/ai-advertising-agency) covers the wider checks, our[AI UGC agency comparison](https://knowlify.com/articles/best-ai-ugc-agencies) lists more providers, and our guide to[UGC usage rights](https://knowlify.com/articles/ugc-usage-rights-explained-for-facebook-ads) explains the terms creators and platforms use.


## Key takeaways


- Ask for ad-file ownership and actor rights as separate clauses.
- A library actor and a custom actor raise different reuse questions.
- EditClub lists ownership of videos and source files, so ask every provider for the same, plus the actor terms.
- Plan for Meta's AI label and the FTC testimonial rule before you film.


## FAQ


### Which AI ad agency is best if I want to own my ads?


Knowlify is our top pick for done-for-you AI video ads, but we cannot cite a published ownership clause for it, so ask for the file and presenter terms in the quote. EditClub is the clearest published example of ownership of videos and source files. Whichever you choose, get the actor terms in writing too.


### Can an AI actor be exclusive to my brand?


Only if the contract says so. Ask whether the actor is built for you, whether other clients can use the same face or voice, and what exclusivity costs. Do not assume a library actor is exclusive to you.


### Do I keep rights to an AI actor after the contract ends?


Not unless the written terms say so. Ask which files you keep, whether existing ads can keep running, and whether you get any continued license to the likeness. Get those answers before the first brief.


### Does owning the ads mean I can run them indefinitely?


Check the usage terms, not just the ownership clause. Common Thread Collective's UGC packages include unlimited paid and organic usage rights, but that describes creator footage, not an AI actor. Confirm duration, channels and whitelisting for AI-made ads as well.


### Does AI disclosure change who owns the ad?


Disclosure and ownership are separate questions. Meta may label ads with a photorealistic AI person, and the FTC's testimonial rule still applies when an avatar delivers the lines. Cover both in the agreement, and take legal advice if the campaign is large.
